policy._why_new_pages_per_week: 6, raised from 2 on 2026-08-29, and judged rather than removed. Three things fix it. (1) It is 24% of refresh_capacity_per_week, so 19 of the 25 declared weekly refresh slots still belong to the 2,262 pages already published - the point of this cap is that new work must not crowd out keeping the tail inside refresh_window_days. (2) It clears a waiting backlog inside one refresh window: the demand-backed lane had 60 measured queries queued behind its own per-run cap and a domain gate, and 60 / 6 is 10 weeks against a 91-day (13-week) window, so no page in a cohort that size ages past the citation threshold before the cohort is finished. The lane's actual composable backlog on this date is 11 pages, which clears in two releases. (3) It still binds: at 6, one release can add at most 0.3% of the library's URLs, so a future demand pull of 200 composable queries lands over 30-odd releases rather than overnight. This number is the single source of truth for both sides. scripts/cadence_gate.js blocks a release whose new-URL count exceeds it, and scripts/programmatic/demand_backed_atoms.mjs spends exactly this budget per run, counted the way the gate counts it: NEW URLs measured against data/cadence/known_urls.json. Re-rendering a page already in that ledger costs nothing, which is what lets a backlog drain across releases instead of the lane being permanently capped at one release's allowance. Raise it here and both move together.
policy._why: 13 weeks is the point where pages become markedly more likely to lose AI citations, and recency is the strongest single correlate of being cited. The ceiling is refresh capacity times that window: publish faster than the library can be maintained and the tail ages out of citability.
policy._provenance_refresh_capacity_per_week: refresh_capacity_per_week is NOT a measurement. It traces to a single unsourced sentence, and no repository in this portfolio has been shown to sustain it; publication and refresh rates observed across the portfolio when this was reviewed on 2026-08-27 ranged roughly 0.4 to 3.2 per week, against the 25 asserted here. The number is left unchanged deliberately - correcting it is a capacity decision, not an editorial one - but every figure derived from it inherits the same standing. maintainable_ceiling is refresh_capacity_per_week * floor(refresh_window_days / 7), so 25 * 13 = 325, and the library_over_ceiling warning reports "N pages cannot be kept current at this capacity" using it. Those outputs look like measurements and are not: they are this figure restated. Read them as "against a declared capacity of 25", never as an observed limit. If the real sustainable rate is established, change it here and every derived ceiling corrects itself.

warnings: library_over_ceiling: 2231 pages against a ceiling of 325 (25 substantive refreshes per week held inside 91 days). 1906 pages cannot be kept current at this capacity.
